John Lothrop Motley reaches the Armada's climax in the second part of chapter nineteen of his History. The English fleet drops anchor near Calais, within a mile and a half of the Spaniards. Lord Henry Seymour's junction completes the combined force. That invincible armada has at last almost reached its destination.

Parma's veterans wait on shore, disciplined on a hundred battlefields, to embark for England. A night of anxiety precedes the fireships and the running fight up the Channel. Motley writes the scene as the hinge of his whole history. The republic's survival, England's safety, and Spain's decline meet off Calais roads. His sympathy is wholly with the defenders. Readers get the campaign from the Dutch side of the water, where small ships and shallow coasts defeated an empire's design.
